R02-F-01: Ask someone to describe the route from their home to the nearest railway station and watch their hands. Before they have finished the first sentence, the hands will usually be tracing turns, marking distances and pointing at landmarks that are nowhere in the room. The common explanation is that gesture is a kind of visual aid for the listener, a way of adding pictures to words. On this view the hands are an accessory to communication, useful when they help an audience and idle otherwise. The explanation is not wrong, but it is incomplete, and the part it leaves out is the more interesting one. If gesture existed only for listeners, people would stop gesturing when nobody could see them, and yet they do not: speakers on the telephone continue to move their hands, if somewhat less than they would face to face, and people who have been blind from birth gesture when they talk, even to listeners they know to be blind. A habit that persists when it can no longer inform anyone is unlikely to be explained entirely by what it does for others. The more economical conclusion is that gesture also does something for the person who produces it. What it seems to do is lighten the work of thinking, for when people are asked to explain a problem while keeping their hands still, many speak more haltingly and struggle to find the words they want, particularly words for shapes, directions and positions. Children explaining how they solved a sum sometimes show with their hands a strategy that their words have not yet reached, pointing to two numbers together while describing a different procedure aloud. Such children are often found to be on the verge of learning the correct method, as if the hands had arrived at an idea before speech could carry it. Gesture, on this account, is not a translation of finished thought into movement; it is one of the places where thought is still being worked out. It would be easy to overstate the case, since not every flourish of the hands is cognitive labour; some gestures are plainly social, like a wave or a shrug, and some speakers gesture little without thinking any worse for it. Nor does the evidence show that thought depends on the body in some mysterious way that rules out abstract reasoning. The claim is more modest: that for many people, much of the time, moving the hands is part of how a difficult idea gets held in mind. Even that modest claim has practical consequences, because a teacher who attends only to what a pupil says may miss what the pupil is close to understanding, and a classroom that rewards stillness may be quietly removing a tool that some children use to think.
R02-F-02: When people imagine an intelligent animal, they usually imagine something built on the plan of their own bodies: a large brain in the head that gathers information, makes decisions and issues commands to obedient limbs. The octopus is a standing challenge to that picture. Its evolutionary line separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently. And it was assembled on a strikingly different plan, for more of the octopus's neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain. The arrangement has consequences that can be observed. An octopus arm can carry out a sequence of movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to draw it in, with little apparent direction from the centre, and an arm separated from the body will for a time continue to respond to touch and to grasp what it meets. Each arm, it seems, handles much of the detail of its own movement, while the central brain sets broader goals. Instead of a commander and its troops, the better image might be a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business. Popular writing has been quick to turn this into a slogan, describing the octopus as an animal with nine brains, or as a colony of minds sharing one body. The slogan goes too far. The arms are not independent agents with purposes of their own; they share a body, a nervous system and, in ordinary life, a single course of action, and the animal behaves as one creature pursuing one end at a time. What the anatomy shows is not that the octopus is many minds but that one mind can be organised so that much of its work is done at the edges. That is the real lesson, and it reaches beyond octopuses. Much thinking about intelligence, in animals and in machines alike, has assumed that it must be centralised: that there must be some single place where everything comes together and is decided. The octopus suggests that centralisation is one solution among several, suited to some bodies and not to others. An animal with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve, since each arm can bend at any point along its length and in any direction. Handing much of the work to the arms may be less an evolutionary curiosity than a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has.
R02-F-03: The mirror test has an appealing simplicity: an animal is given a mark it cannot see directly, perhaps a spot of odourless dye on the forehead, and is then shown a mirror. If it uses the reflection to inspect or rub at the mark on its own body, it is said to recognise itself. Great apes generally pass, most monkeys generally fail, and over the decades a handful of other species have been reported to pass or nearly pass. Because the result is so easy to state, it has come to be treated as a kind of membership test: those who pass belong among the self-aware, and those who fail are presumed to lack a self worth the name. The test does measure something real. To pass, an animal must grasp that the moving figure in the glass is not another individual and that what it sees there corresponds to its own body. That is not a trivial achievement, and it is reasonable to think that animals capable of it have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others. The difficulty lies in what is inferred from failure, and in how much is read into success. Consider failure first, since the test presupposes an animal that relies heavily on vision, that attends to its own appearance, and that is bothered enough by an odd mark to investigate it. Many animals meet none of these conditions. A dog, which navigates its world largely by smell, may simply have no interest in a silent image that gives off no scent; an animal whose species does not groom may see no reason to touch a spot on its skin. Failing a test designed around one animal's priorities is weak evidence that another animal lacks the capacity being tested, in the way that a person's failure to answer a question asked in an unfamiliar language reveals little about her knowledge. Success is open to over-reading too. Recognising one's body in a mirror shows an understanding of the body as one's own; it does not show, by itself, that the animal reflects on its past, imagines its future or thinks of itself as a person with a history. These are richer capacities, and the leap from the mirror to them is a leap of interpretation, not of evidence. None of this makes the test worthless. It makes it one probe among many, informative within its range and silent outside it. The error is not in running the test but in letting a single, visually biased procedure decide which minds are admitted to the category of the self-aware.
R02-F-04: It has become a commonplace that every age describes the brain in the image of its most impressive machine. When ornamental gardens were fitted with water-driven statues that moved as visitors stepped on hidden plates, nerves were pictured as pipes and the animal spirits as fluid pressed through them. When the telegraph and then the telephone exchange spread across cities, the nervous system became a network of wires, with the brain as the central office where calls were connected. In our own time it is a computer, processing information, storing memories and running programs. The pattern is real, and critics have drawn a sharp lesson from it: the metaphors are fashions, each as quaint as the last will soon appear, and the computer image will go the way of the fountain. The lesson is half right. It is true that none of these images was the whole truth, and that each looks dated once the technology behind it is familiar. But to call them mere fashions is to miss what each one got right. The hydraulic picture captured the idea that something must travel from the senses to the centre and back to the muscles. The switchboard captured the importance of connections, of which signal is routed to which destination. The computer captured the idea that what matters about these signals is the information they carry and the transformations performed on it, rather than the stuff that carries them. Each metaphor, in other words, was adopted because it made some feature of the nervous system thinkable, and each left behind a contribution that survived its own retirement. The real danger lies elsewhere, because a metaphor brings with it not only the features that fit but a whole set of features that come along unexamined. The computer image invites us to think of memory as storage, a place where a record sits unchanged until retrieved, when remembering appears to be closer to reconstruction, the record altered a little each time it is used. It invites a sharp division between hardware and software, when in the brain the program and the machine are hard to tell apart, since use reshapes the very structures that do the work. These are not reasons to abandon the metaphor but reasons to keep asking which of its features we are actually entitled to. The sensible course, then, is neither to treat the current metaphor as a literal description nor to dismiss it as a passing fashion, but to use it while keeping an account of where it fails. Metaphors are tools for thinking about something that cannot be seen directly, and the history of brain science suggests that thinking without any of them is not an available option. What can be avoided is the habit of mistaking the tool for the thing.
R02-F-05: Among the people who first tried to build thinking machines, a surprise emerged that has never quite been absorbed. The tasks that seemed to demand the most intelligence, such as proving theorems, playing chess or solving problems in algebra, turned out to be comparatively tractable for computers, while tasks that any small child performs without effort, such as recognising a face across a room, picking up an unfamiliar object or walking over uneven ground, proved stubbornly hard. The observation is often associated with the roboticist Hans Moravec, and it is usually called a paradox. Whether it deserves the name depends on what we took difficulty to be in the first place. The most common explanation is evolutionary. Seeing, grasping and moving have been refined over hundreds of millions of years of animal life, and the machinery that performs them is vast, ancient and almost entirely hidden from awareness. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is a recent arrival, practised deliberately and with effort. We notice the effort and conclude that reasoning is hard; we notice nothing when we recognise a friend's face, and conclude that perception is easy. On this account the paradox is an artefact of introspection: our sense of difficulty tracks how much of a skill reaches consciousness, not how much computation it requires. This explanation is persuasive, but it should not be stretched into the claim that every skill we find effortless is computationally deep, or that every skill we find laborious is shallow. Some effortless skills may be easy for machines too, and some laborious ones, like long division, are trivial for any pocket calculator while others remain hard. The evolutionary story explains a general tendency; it does not supply a rule. Nor has the gap stood still. Machines have become far better at recognising images and speech than early researchers expected, though a robot that can fold an unfamiliar garment or clear an untidy table remains much harder to build than a program that plays chess at a master's level. The deeper lesson concerns our idea of intelligence itself. For a long time intelligence was identified with the activities that educated adults found hardest and prized most: calculation, logic, formal games. The paradox suggests that this identification was parochial. What humans find hard is a measure of human limitations, not a measure of how much intelligence a task needs, and the competences we share with other animals may contain more of what is difficult about minds than the competences that distinguish us. A cat crossing a cluttered shelf without disturbing anything is solving problems that our best machines still find formidable, and it would be odd to call that achievement unintelligent merely because no cat could sit an examination.
R02-F-06: The claim that language shapes thought has had an unusual career. In its strong form, the view that the categories of one's language set the limits of what one can perceive or conceive, it was once fashionable, then thoroughly discredited, and it is now defended by almost nobody. The objections are familiar. Speakers of languages that lack a word for some distinction can usually learn to make it when they need to; translation, though imperfect, is possible; and people routinely think thoughts for which they struggle to find words. If a language were a prison, its inmates would not so regularly be found outside the walls. From the ruins of the strong view a weaker one has been rebuilt, and the evidence for it is more respectable. Colour has been the favoured test case, because the spectrum is continuous while languages divide it differently: some have only a few basic colour terms, others a dozen. In one well-known kind of experiment, speakers of a language that has separate basic words for lighter and darker blue were found to be slightly quicker at telling apart two blues that fell on opposite sides of that boundary than two blues on the same side, while speakers of a language with a single basic word for blue showed no such advantage. The effect was modest, but it was there, and it seemed to show that words reach down into perception. What the same line of work also found, however, is more revealing than the effect itself. When participants performed the colour task while silently rehearsing a string of digits, which occupies the verbal system, the advantage largely disappeared, whereas a comparable task that occupied spatial memory instead left it intact. The words, it seems, were not permanently altering how the visual system sorted colours. They were being used, there and then, as an aid to the task, recruited on the spot and set aside when the verbal system was busy elsewhere. Defenders and critics of linguistic relativity have both tended to miss what this implies. The defenders read such results as vindication: language shapes thought after all. The critics read the smallness of the effects as deflation: language barely matters. But the finding fits neither reading well. It suggests that language does not so much reshape a mind that would otherwise be neutral as serve as one of the instruments a mind reaches for while it works. On this picture the interesting question is not whether a speaker's language has engraved its categories on her perception, but how often, and in which tasks, thinking proceeds by borrowing words as tools. That question is in one respect more modest than the relativists' and in another more radical, since it implies that much ordinary thought is partly carried out in language even where we take it to be wordless.
R02-F-07: In the 1890s the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan proposed a rule for interpreting animal behaviour that has shaped the study of animal minds ever since. In paraphrase, it says that we should not explain an animal's action as the product of a higher mental faculty if it can be explained as the product of a lower one. The rule was a response to a real problem. Much of what then passed for evidence about animal intelligence consisted of anecdotes sent in by pet owners and naturalists, in which dogs reasoned, cats planned and birds grieved, and in which the observer's own feelings were read into whatever the animal happened to do. Against this habit, Morgan's canon was a discipline: before crediting a creature with insight, ask whether trial and error, habit or simple association would account for what you saw. As a corrective, the canon did its work well. It pushed the field towards controlled observation and towards explanations that could be tested, and it is partly responsible for the expectation that claims about animal cognition must now survive experiments designed to rule out simpler accounts. But a rule that is useful against one error can become an error of its own when it is applied without thought. Over the following century the canon hardened, in many hands, into a presumption that the lowest available explanation is always to be preferred, whatever the animal and whatever the evidence. The trouble with that presumption is that it is not as neutral as it looks. It treats 'lower' as if it meant 'simpler' and 'simpler' as if it meant 'more probably true', and neither equation holds in general. An explanation in terms of association may require positing a long and improbable history of exactly the right rewards, while an explanation in terms of a modest capacity to represent what another animal can see may be the more economical of the two. Evolution complicates the picture further. If a chimpanzee and a human behave alike in similar circumstances, the assumption that the behaviour rests on similar mechanisms is, given their close kinship, arguably the simpler hypothesis; to insist on a different and lower mechanism for the chimpanzee alone is to multiply explanations, not to reduce them. There is also a question of cost. The canon guards against one kind of mistake, crediting animals with capacities they lack, and is silent about the opposite mistake, denying them capacities they have. Both mistakes are real, and the second is not obviously the less harmful, especially where the capacities in question include the ability to suffer. An investigator who refuses on principle to credit a dog with fear until every leaner account has been excluded will seldom be caught overstating anything, but she may spend a career understating what is in front of her. A principle that treats one error as serious and the other as negligible is not a principle of caution; it is a bias that happens to look like one. None of this is a case for returning to the anecdote. Morgan himself appears to have intended his rule as a guard against careless inference rather than as a ban on crediting animals with higher faculties when there is independent evidence for them. The better successor to the canon is not its opposite but a symmetrical standard: state the rival hypotheses, rich and lean alike, and design observations that would tell them apart. Simplicity then becomes something to be argued for in each case, rather than a verdict delivered in advance.
R02-F-08: Any science of consciousness faces an awkward fact at its foundation. The thing it studies is, by most accounts, directly available only to the person who has it, and the scientist learns about it chiefly through what that person says or otherwise signals: I saw the flash, or I did not; the face looked angry; the tone seemed to come from the left. Two opposite attitudes to this fact have been common. One holds that reports are so unreliable, so shaped by expectation, vocabulary and the wish to please, that a science resting on them is no science at all. The other treats a sincere report as the last word, since no one, it is said, is better placed than the subject to know what she experiences. Neither attitude survives inspection, and the second is the easier to dismiss. People are often wrong about their own experience in ways that can be demonstrated: they confidently describe detail at the edges of their visual field that is not available to them, and they misjudge the order or timing of events they claim to have perceived. A report is a response produced by the subject, shaped by the question asked and the categories available, and it can misdescribe the experience it is about. But the first attitude draws the wrong conclusion from this. Every scientific instrument can misreport what it measures; the usual response is to study its errors, not to throw it away. A report is best treated as evidence about experience, fallible but informative, to be calibrated against other evidence rather than either revered or ignored. The most productive methods have used reports in exactly this spirit. In masking experiments, the same image is shown on many trials, sometimes followed so quickly by a second image that the first is not reported as seen. Because the physical stimulus is held constant, differences in brain activity between seen and unseen trials can be attributed, at least tentatively, to the difference in experience rather than to the stimulus. The approach is powerful, but it carries a hidden complication. On seen trials the subject not only experiences the image but also prepares and makes a report about it, so some of the activity that distinguishes the two kinds of trial may belong to reporting rather than to experiencing. To get around this, researchers have designed experiments in which subjects make no report at all, and conscious states are inferred from other signs, such as involuntary eye movements that track which of two competing images is being experienced. Critics point out a circle here: those signs were themselves validated by showing that they agree with reports. If reports are suspect, so, it seems, are the signs that stand in for them. The objection is clever, but it proves less than it appears to. The history of measurement is full of such circles. Early thermometers were checked against the sensation of warmth and then against one another, and in time they came to correct the very sensations against which they had first been checked. A circle of mutual calibration is vicious only if it never widens; when independent methods, each imperfect, are tested against one another and turn out to agree, confidence in all of them can rise together. None of this guarantees that a science of consciousness will answer every question asked of it, and some philosophers doubt that any amount of correlating brain activity with reports could explain why experience exists at all. That doubt may be justified. But it is a doubt about the reach of the science, not about whether reports can serve as its data, and running the two together has done more to obscure the field than either the sceptics or the enthusiasts have usually admitted.
